transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
The Supreme Court has denied a last-minute request from the Department of Justice to wade into its unprecedented feud with California over the state's voter rolls.
NPR's Jude Joffe Block reports the denial comes just hours after the Justice Department filed its appeal.
The Justice Department wanted the high court to force California election officials to set aside ballots that pertain to 20,000 people that federal officials say are likely non-citizens.
But California election officials and data experts have argued the DOJ's list is full of errors.
Plus, they've said segregating ballots isn't feasible with voting already underway.
The Supreme Court's refusal to take on the case comes after both a federal judge and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the DOJ's demand last week, citing that the Constitution gives states authority to run elections.
Plus, federal courts tend to avoid changing voting rules right before an election.
Jude Joffe Block, NPR News.
President Trump delivered his last public address ahead of the midterm elections today.
Trump promised to campaign in key swing districts, but the political ground shifted under him, and the bulk of his rallies have been in Republican states, where he won big just two years ago, as NPR's Tamara Keith explains.
There's little question that the president is going to own the outcome of these midterms.
I am not predicting that he will take responsibility if Republicans lose, but he's the one who pushed the mid-decade redistricting of House districts.
He picked some of the Senate candidates who were causing the biggest headaches for Republicans, Michael Watley in North Carolina, Darlene Graham in South Carolina, and the scandal-plagued Ken Paxton in Texas.
That race alone is up to nearly $600 million in spending on air, according to Ad Impact.
Republicans should not have to sink more than $400 million into a Senate race in Texas, of all places.
NPR's Tamara Keith reporting. Recent developments in mRNA vaccines have shown promised fighting cancer.
NPR's Yuki Noguchi reports researchers are trying to figure out how to learn what's behind some recent successful trials.
Seven years ago, Donna Gustafson received the world's first mRNA vaccine against pancreatic cancer.
I had no symptoms, no side effects, to the point where I was actually worried that maybe it was not helping.
But it has. Gustafson has lived cancer-free since.
The personalized vaccine used samples of her tumor to genetically reprogram immune cells to recognize distinctive proteins on her cancerous cells and kill them.
Similar vaccines are being tested on lung, kidney, bladder, and brain cancers.
But researchers don't yet understand why some trials have failed, while others are showing radical results. Yuki Noguchi, NPR News.
Major U.S. stock indexes closed mixed today as tech and AI stocks remained shaky following their sell-off last week.
This is NPR.
The FDA has approved a generic version of the world's only twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV.
It's a big step toward making the extremely effective drug available inexpensively and quickly in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
The drug, called Lenacapivir, is expected to cost $40 a person, the same price as daily preventative pills available now.
A federal trial has begun for two pitchers for the Cleveland Guardians, who are accused of accepting bribes to rig pitches for gamblers.
Jury selection began today, as NPR's Becky Sullivan reports.
Cleveland's all-star pitcher, Emmanuel Klase, was one of the best closers in baseball when prosecutors say he threw at least 18 rigged pitches.
All of them, the first pitch of the ninth inning, all of them in the dirt, are far off the plate.
Betters allegedly won at least $460,000 by placing scores of total wagers, making specific bets about those pitches.
Prosecutors say the scheme lasted for at least two years.
Another Guardians pitcher, Luis Ortiz, is accused of throwing rigged pitches at two games in 2025.
The trial is expected to last about a month.
Witnesses will include teammates and baseball executives.
Both players have pleaded not guilty to charges of fraud, sports, bribery, and money laundering.
If convicted, they face decades of prison time.
Becky Sullivan, NPR News.
Carl Buschby completed an epic walk around the world that he started in 1998.
The former British paratrooper was 29 then and is now 57.
He navigated a frigid, bearing strait, swam the Caspian Sea, and crossed the English Channel.
He faced geopolitical conflicts, harsh weather, and personal challenges,
but finally made it back to his mom's home in Hull, England.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Supreme Court denies Justice Department request to intervene in California voter roll dispute
Trump delivers final public address before midterms and campaigns mainly in Republican states
Researchers investigate why some mRNA cancer vaccine trials succeed while others fail
Major U.S. stock indexes close mixed as tech and AI stocks remain shaky after sell-off
FDA approves generic twice-a-year HIV prevention shot Lenacapavir for low- and middle-income countries
Federal trial begins for Cleveland Guardians pitchers accused of rigging pitches for gamblers
British adventurer Carl Bushby completes round-the-world walk started in 1998 in Hull
